questions.question: What distinguishes observability from monitoring known conditions?
options: Observability stores only traces instead of metrics
Observability supports asking new questions about internal state from system evidence
Observability removes the need for service ownership
Observability guarantees every event is retained forever
questions.explanation: Monitoring checks anticipated conditions; observability preserves connected evidence so responders can investigate failures they did not predict.

questions.question: Why is request_id a dangerous metric label?
options: Counters cannot contain labels
It creates an unbounded label value set and can explode active series
It prevents metrics from having timestamps
It forces every trace to use tail sampling
questions.explanation: Unique values multiply the number of active time series. Keep identity in logs or traces and use bounded metric dimensions.

questions.question: A 99.9% SLO permits a 0.1% error rate. The current error rate is 1%. What is the burn rate?
options: 1x
questions.explanation: Burn rate is observed error fraction divided by allowed error fraction: 1% divided by 0.1% equals 10x.

questions.question: Which trace sampling policy can deliberately retain errors after the outcome is known?
options: Random head sampling
Outcome-aware tail sampling
Metric downsampling
Log rotation
questions.explanation: Tail sampling waits for enough of the trace to be observed, allowing errors and slow traces to be retained while healthy traffic is sampled.

questions.question: Which investigation sequence most directly connects a user symptom to a safe mitigation?
options: Search every log, inspect CPU, then guess which deploy changed
Outcome SLI, representative trace, structured event, then version and owner
Host disk graph, raw payload dump, then restart every service
Debug logging, longer retention, then a generic dashboard
questions.explanation: The sequence narrows the affected journey, localizes the path, explains the local decision, and connects it to a responsible change.

questions.question: What should an application do when its telemetry backend is unavailable?
options: Block every user request until export succeeds
Drop all evidence silently
Use bounded asynchronous export and expose loss without failing the business operation
Write customer payloads into metric labels
questions.explanation: Telemetry must not become a critical dependency of the business path, but bounded queues, drop counters, and an independent signal must make degradation visible.

questions.question: Why pair a short high-burn window with a longer alert window?
options: To page on every transient resource spike
To detect severe budget consumption quickly and confirm that it persists
To replace an SLI with raw CPU utilization
To make the error budget larger
questions.explanation: The short window provides speed, while the longer window reduces noise by confirming sustained error-budget consumption.

questions.question: Which signal reveals a collector blind spot rather than real traffic loss?
options: A fall in one backend's received events with stable independent edge request counts
A matching fall in edge traffic and completed business outcomes
A planned reduction in retention
A lower debug log level
questions.explanation: Reconciling independent traffic counts with received telemetry distinguishes actual traffic loss from an instrumentation or export failure.
